sponsor_and_incentive: Academic work. Guilford's factor-analytic research programme (the Aptitudes Project at the University of Southern California) was largely funded by US military agencies (the 1970 Vernon introduction notes his work was done 'in military establishments' [uncertain on exact funders, not checked]). No commercial incentive bearing on the definitions. APA publishes the dictionary; no conflict relevant here.
exact_quotes: Guilford 1967, p. 213 (Ch. 10 'Categories of operation', section 'Divergent production'): 'A formal definition of "divergent production" reads: generation of information from given information, where the emphasis is upon variety and quantity of output from the same source; likely to involve transfer. This definition arose directly from consideration of the kinds of tests needed to measure the various divergent-production abilities.'

Guilford 1967, p. 215 (Ch. 10, 'Deduction and convergent production'): 'We might say that in divergent production we are generating the logical possibilities from given information, whereas in convergent production we are generating logical necessities.'

Guilford 1967, pp. 214-215 (Ch. 10, 'Comparisons of convergent and divergent production'): 'In convergent production, the problem can be rigorously structured and is so structured, and an answer is forthcoming without much hesitation. In the former case, restrictions are few; in the latter they are many. In the former, the search is broad; in the latter it is narrow. In the former, output is in quantity; in the latter it is limited. In the former, criteria for success are vague and somewhat lax and may, indeed, stress variety and quantity; in the latter, criteria are sharper, more rigorous, and demanding.'

Guilford 1967, p. 215: 'In everyday life, of course, the middle ground between these two kinds of functioning is not excluded, and the individual very frequently engages in much divergent production on the way to a convergent answer, as when he puzzles over a mathematical problem and tries one solution after another.'

Guilford 1967, p. 62 (Ch. 3, origin of the terms): 'so a class of factors was given the title of "divergent-thinking" abilities. The representative tests are all of completion form, and the examinee makes a good score for the number and variety of his responses and sometimes for high quality. ... A set of these abilities, parallel to the divergent-thinking abilities, suggested the title of "convergent thinking"; in accordance with the information given in the item, the examinee must converge upon the one right answer. To avoid the ambiguity of the term thinking, the later substitution of the term production was made. Thus, two operation categories, divergent production and convergent production, were adopted.'

Guilford 1967, start of Ch. 7 'Convergent-production abilities' (c. p. 171 [uncertain page]): 'Convergent production is in the area of logical deductions or at least the area of compelling inferences. Convergent production rather than divergent production is the prevailing function when the input information is sufficient to determine a unique answer.'

Guilford 1967, p. 138 (Ch. 6 'Divergent-production abilities'): 'Divergent production is a concept defined in accordance with a set of factors of intellectual ability that pertain primarily to information retrieval and with their tests, which call for a number of varied responses to each test item.'

Guilford 1959, 'Traits of creativity' (Vernon 1970 reprint, p. 179-180): 'Convergent thinking proceeds toward a restricted answer or solution. If asked: "What is the opposite of high?" you would probably respond with "Low." This is an example of convergent thinking. ... But if you were asked to give a number of words that mean about the same as "low", you could produce several different responses, all satisfying the requirement, such as "depressed", "cheap", "degraded", and the like, and you would be correct. In this example we have an instance of divergent thinking.'

Guilford 1959 (Vernon reprint, summary section, c. p. 183-184): 'Most of the aptitude factors identifiable as belonging in the category of creativity are classifiable in a group of divergent-thinking abilities. These abilities, by contrast to convergent-thinking abilities, emphasize searching activities with freedom to go in different directions, if not a necessity to do so in order to achieve an excellent performance. Convergent-thinking activities proceed toward one right answer, or one that is more or less clearly demanded by the given information.'

Guilford 1959 (Vernon reprint, p. 176): 'Convergent thinking, which will be more fully explained in the next section, involves thinking toward one right answer, or toward a relatively uniquely determined answer. A companion factor was defined as an interest in or liking for divergent thinking, a type of thinking in which considerable searching about is done and a number of answers will do.'

Guilford 1959 (Vernon reprint, p. 180): 'We might arbitrarily define creative thinking as divergent thinking, but it would be incorrect to say that divergent thinking accounts for all the intellectual components of creative production.'

APA Dictionary, 'convergent production': 'the capacity to produce the right answer to a question or to choose the best solution to a problem. It is one of the abilities recognized in the structure of intellect model.'
APA Dictionary, 'divergent production': 'the capacity to produce novel solutions to a problem. It is one of the abilities recognized in the structure of intellect model.'

APA Dictionary, 'convergent thinking': 'critical thinking in which an individual uses linear, logical steps to analyze a number of already formulated solutions to a problem to determine the correct one or the one that is most likely to be successful. Compare divergent thinking. [defined in 1967 by Joy Paul Guilford]'

APA Dictionary, 'divergent thinking': 'creative thinking in which an individual solves a problem or reaches a decision using strategies that deviate from commonly used or previously taught strategies. This term is often used synonymously with lateral thinking. Compare convergent thinking. [defined in 1967 by Joy Paul Guilford]'

APA Dictionary, 'structure of intellect model (SOI)': 'a model of intelligence that postulates five operations (cognition, memory, divergent production, convergent production, evaluation), six products ..., and five contents ..., for a total of 150 separate factors of intelligence (120 in an earlier version of the theory). The evidence for the theory is weak and in large part was refuted by the work of U.S. psychologist John L. Horn (1928-2006). ... [initially proposed in the 1950s by Joy Paul Guilford]'

Vernon 1970, editor's introduction, p. 11 (paraphrase of Guilford 1950, not Guilford's words): 'Another turning point was J. P. Guilford's (1950) paper which pointed out that almost all the tests and achievement examinations used by American psychologists and educationists were "convergent", that is, for each item there was one predetermined correct answer. ... Creative thought is more likely to issue in a variety of new answers, in other words, to be divergent.'
date_and_recency: Guilford's definitions: 1959 chapter and 1967 monograph; the 1950 address set out the creativity hypotheses that led to the work. Per Guilford 1967 p. 62, the terms began as 'convergent thinking' and 'divergent thinking' and were later renamed 'production'. APA Dictionary entries updated 19 April 2018, retrieved 21 November 2026. A conceptual source, so no AI model period applies.
key_claims: Guilford (1967) formally defines divergent production as 'generation of information from given information, where the emphasis is upon variety and quantity of output from the same source; likely to involve transfer'. Convergent production also generates information from given information, but it is the 'prevailing function when the input information is sufficient to determine a unique answer'. It is the home of deduction: divergent production generates 'logical possibilities', convergent production 'logical necessities'. In convergent production the problem is rigorously structured, the search narrow, output limited and success criteria sharp. Divergent tasks are loose, the search broad, output plentiful and criteria lax. The two are not exclusive: people often use 'much divergent production on the way to a convergent answer'. In 1959 Guilford put it in plain terms: convergent thinking 'proceed[s] toward one right answer, or one that is more or less clearly demanded by the given information', while divergent-thinking abilities 'emphasize searching activities with freedom to go in different directions'. He linked creativity mainly to divergent thinking but warned it would be 'incorrect to say that divergent thinking accounts for all the intellectual components of creative production'. Both are two of five operations in his structure-of-intellect (SI) model. The definitions were drawn from the tests used to measure the abilities ('This definition arose directly from consideration of the kinds of tests needed').
headline_figures: SI model: five operations, six products, contents (four in 1967: figural, symbolic, semantic, behavioral), giving 120 hypothesised abilities in the 1967 version; APA Dictionary: 150 factors in the later version ('120 in an earlier version of the theory'). Guilford 1967 Ch. 7: 'Of the 24 hypothesized [convergent-production] abilities, 13 have not been investigated.' Guilford 1959: interest-inventory correlations with fluency, flexibility and originality test scores were statistically significant 'but the coefficients were all below 0.30'.
sample_and_method: Factor analysis of batteries of psychometric aptitude tests, mostly given to adults (many in military and USAF samples) and later to schoolchildren, in Guilford's Aptitudes Research Project. Convergent and divergent were defined by test format: completion items scored for the number and variety of responses (divergent) versus items with one specified right answer (convergent). Not a study of software engineers.
what_is_measured: Two intellectual operations. Convergent production: producing the one correct or logically required answer from the given information (deduction). Divergent production: producing many varied candidate answers from the given information (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration). This maps onto the angle as follows: a classic coding test with one correct, testable output is a convergent-production task in Guilford's sense.
validity_evidence: None for coding interviews. Guilford 1959 (Vernon reprint, c. p. 182) cites only small criterion correlations, all from Guilford 1956a: ideational fluency 0.37 with 'performance of aircraft engineers whose chief work was in designing aircraft parts', where the criterion was 'rate of increase in pay over a limited period of time'; adaptive flexibility 0.31 with the same criterion; expressional fluency 0.25 with astronomy grades 'for some unknown reason'. Uncorrected r, small samples not stated in the reprint. The APA Dictionary calls the evidence for the overall SI theory 'weak'.
relevance_to_angle: Supports 'stop testing convergent coding' by giving the term a precise, citable origin. In Guilford's words, a convergent task is one where 'the input information is sufficient to determine a unique answer', with 'one right answer, or one that is more or less clearly demanded by the given information'. That describes a LeetCode-style problem with a fixed correct output, which an agent can now produce. Design conversation and directing an agent lean on divergent production (generating several possibilities) and evaluation (judging them), which is a separate SI operation. There is a complication: Guilford says people use 'much divergent production on the way to a convergent answer', so even a convergent coding test involves some divergent search. Calling it purely convergent is a simplification. Also, Guilford's 'evaluation' operation, not divergent production, is the closer fit for reviewing agent output.
limitations_stated: Guilford 1967 p. 215: the convergent/divergent contrasts 'reflect the contrasts between the kinds of test that have worked best for the two kinds of production abilities', and 'the middle ground between these two kinds of functioning is not excluded'. In tests there is 'sometimes a twilight region, if not an apparent continuum' (Ch. 7). Guilford 1959: 'it would be incorrect to say that divergent thinking accounts for all the intellectual components of creative production.' Guilford 1967 Ch. 7: convergent production 'is one of the less explored regions of intelligence', with 13 of 24 hypothesised abilities uninvestigated.
counter_evidence: APA Dictionary: 'The evidence for the theory is weak and in large part was refuted by the work of U.S. psychologist John L. Horn (1928-2006).' Horn and Knapp (1973) argued that Guilford's targeted rotations would support almost any hypothesised factors [uncertain: not opened]. The APA's own 'convergent thinking' entry ('analyze a number of already formulated solutions ... to determine the correct one') describes selecting among given options, which is not Guilford's definition (generating the uniquely determined answer). Its 'divergent thinking' entry ('strategies that deviate from commonly used or previously taught strategies', 'synonymously with lateral thinking') also drifts from his 'variety and quantity of output'. So quote Guilford 1967 for definitions, not the APA 'thinking' entries, even though those carry a '[defined in 1967 by Joy Paul Guilford]' tag. The 1967 date is also loose: Guilford was using both terms in print by 1959.
verification_status: Verified against opened primary sources: 1967 formal divergent production definition (p. 213); 'logical possibilities ... logical necessities' (p. 215); the contrast list (pp. 214-215); origin of the terms and the renaming from 'thinking' to 'production' (p. 62); 'prevailing function when the input information is sufficient to determine a unique answer' (Ch. 7, page c. 171 [uncertain]); the 1959 'one right answer' and 'freedom to go in different directions' wording (Vernon reprint). Verified against the opened encyclopaedic source: all five APA Dictionary entries, verbatim. Not verified: what the 1950 American Psychologist paper itself says. Vernon's statement that it called tests 'convergent' is a secondary paraphrase, and Guilford may not have used the words 'convergent' or 'divergent' in 1950 [uncertain]. Do not attribute the terms to the 1950 paper without opening it. No formal one-line definition of convergent production matching the divergent one was found in the 1967 text. The closest Guilford wording is the Ch. 7 and p. 215 sentences above [uncertain whether a formal definition exists elsewhere in the book].
